opener.display: Here is a hill built out of four flat slices, each one 10 m thick. On the right, the same hill has been drawn from directly above.

steps.say: No method yet. Just look and count.

steps.pre: Each slice is 10 m thick and there are 4 of them. Type the height of the top of the hill, in metres.
steps.done: You have just read a height from a stack of layers, which is all a contour map is.

steps.pre: Now look at the same hill drawn from above. Type how many rings you can count.
steps.hint: There is one outline for the edge of each slice.
steps.done: One ring per slice, and the smallest ring is the top slice.

steps.say: Those rings are contour lines. Every line joins ground at the same height, and the height goes up one step for every ring you move inwards. Where the slices are steep the rings crowd together, and where the ground is gentle they spread out. This lesson reads those lines: the numbers on them, the gaps between them, and the shapes they make.

bronze.display: A small hill on a map. The number printed on the outer ring is a height in metres, and the contour interval here is 10 m.

steps.say: Locate the feature first. Reading comes second.

steps.pre: The rings sit between two vertical grid lines. Type the easting of the line on the left of that square.
steps.hint: The eastings are printed under the grid lines, reading 21, 22, 23.
steps.done: The hill is pinned to a square, so nothing that follows can be read off the wrong feature.

steps.pre: Type the number printed on the outer ring, in metres.
steps.hint: It sits in a gap in the outer line so the line stays readable.

steps.pre: The interval is 10 m. Type the height of the middle ring, in metres.
steps.hint: One step inwards is one step uphill.

steps.pre: Type the height of the smallest ring, in metres.
steps.hint: Another step inwards, another interval up.

steps.pre: Type 1 if the ground inside the smallest ring is the highest ground here, or 2 if it is the lowest.
steps.hint: The rings get smaller as the land climbs.
steps.done: The top of any hill is inside the smallest ring, which is why you count inwards.

steps.say: Bronze move: find the feature, read the printed number as a height, then step by the interval.

silver.display: Part of a slope. The two thick lines are index contours and they are labelled. Four thin lines are drawn between them.

steps.say: The interval is almost never printed. Two labelled lines will give it to you.

steps.pre: Type how many lines are drawn on this slope altogether, thick and thin.
steps.hint: Count every line from the left-hand edge of the slope across to the right-hand edge.
steps.done: Knowing how many lines there are stops you losing count part way through.

steps.pre: Type the height labelled on the left-hand thick line, in metres.
steps.hint: It is printed under the thick line on the lower side of the slope.
steps.done: One known height at each end is the evidence the whole calculation needs.

steps.pre: Type the height difference between the two thick lines, in metres.
steps.hint: Take the smaller label away from the larger one.

steps.pre: Type how many thin lines are drawn between them.
steps.hint: Count only the thin lines, not the thick ones.

steps.pre: Type how many equal steps that makes from the lower thick line up to the higher one.
steps.hint: Four lines in between create one more gap than there are lines.

steps.pre: Share the height difference between those steps. Type the contour interval, in metres.
steps.hint: Divide the difference by the number of steps.
steps.done: Interval found, so now any unlabelled line on this map can be given a height.

steps.say: Silver move: lines plus one create the steps, and the height difference shared over those steps is the interval.

gold.display: A slope seen from the side. A walker goes from A up to B, and the ground distance between them is marked underneath.

steps.say: Gradient needs two things only: how much you go up, and how far you go along.

steps.pre: Type the height at A, in metres.
steps.hint: It is written beside the lower point.
steps.done: Both ends read off the diagram before any arithmetic starts.

steps.pre: Type the height at B, in metres.
steps.hint: It is written beside the higher point.

steps.pre: Type the height climbed, in metres.
steps.hint: Take the lower height away from the higher one.

steps.pre: The ground distance is 0.4 km. Divide the climb by it. Type the gradient in metres per km.
steps.hint: Eighty metres of climb shared over four tenths of a kilometre.

steps.pre: Now turn 0.4 km into metres. Type the answer.
steps.hint: One kilometre is one thousand metres.

steps.pre: Divide the metres along by the metres up. Type the figure that finishes 1 in this.
steps.hint: Four hundred along shared into eighty up.
steps.done: Metres per km and a 1 in ratio describe the same slope, so a sensible answer to one checks the other.

steps.say: Gold move: rise over distance in km gives metres per km, and rise over distance in metres gives the 1 in ratio.

method_card.title: Contours & Relief
steps: Locate the feature on the grid before you read any brown line
Read a printed contour number: it is a height in metres above sea level
Use the interval to count up or down from a labelled line
Close lines mean steep ground, spread lines mean gentle ground
method_card.content:
What a contour is. A brown line joining ground of equal height. The number printed on it is that height in metres. Thicker index contours are labelled more often, usually every 50 m.

Interval. The height gap between neighbouring lines. Find it by counting the thin lines between two labelled thick ones, adding one, then sharing the height difference over those steps.

Shapes. Rings inside rings are a hill. Vs pointing upstream are a valley. Rounded points facing downhill are a spur. Almost no lines means flat ground.

Gradient. Height gained divided by distance travelled.
method_card.example:
Question: A hill has a ring labelled 200 m with one smaller ring inside it. The interval is 10 m. How high is the inner ring?

Inwards is uphill, so add one interval: 200 + 10.

Answer: 210 m.

bronze.title: Bronze: Reading the lines the map prints
steps: Find the feature on the grid first, using the numbers along the edges. Only then look at the brown lines.
A number printed on a brown line is a height above sea level in metres, not a distance.
Rings inside rings mean a hill, and the smallest ring is the top of it.
Contours packed close together mean a steep slope. Contours spread far apart mean a gentle one.

example.question: A brown line on a map has 300 printed on it. What does that number tell you?

steps.label: Find where the number sits
steps.content: It is printed in brown, in a gap in the line itself.

steps.label: Decide what it measures
steps.content: Contour numbers are heights above sea level, measured in metres.

steps.label: Check it makes sense
steps.content: Every point along that one line is at the same height, which is why the line can wander.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The land all along that line is 300 m above sea level.

silver.title: Silver: Heights the map does not print
steps: The contour interval is the height gap between one line and the next. Thicker index contours are usually 50 m apart.
Count the thin lines between two labelled thick ones, add one for the last step, then share the height difference over those steps.
Count outwards or inwards from a labelled line, adding the interval going uphill and taking it away going downhill.

example.question: Two thick lines are labelled 100 m and 150 m, with 4 thin lines between them. What is the contour interval?

steps.label: Count the steps
steps.content: 4 thin lines make 5 steps from one thick line to the other.

steps.label: Check it makes sense
steps.content: 5 equal steps must add up to the 50 m difference.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 50 ÷ 5 = 10 m

gold.title: Gold: Gradient and cross sections
steps: Gradient is height gained divided by distance travelled, so keep the distance in the unit the answer asks for.
For metres per km, put the rise in metres over the distance in km. For a ratio, turn the distance into metres and write it as 1 in something.
A cross section rises where contour values climb and falls where they drop, and the same values repeat either side of a summit.

example.question: A slope climbs 75 m over 0.6 km. Give the gradient in metres per km and as a ratio.

steps.label: Convert for the ratio
steps.content: 0.6 km = 600 m along the ground

steps.label: Check it makes sense
steps.content: 600 m along for 75 m up is 8 m along for every 1 m up.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 125 m per km, or 1 in 8

exam_context.paper: Map and fieldwork skills questions, on whichever paper your board sets them
exam_context.marks: Short answers: give the height with its unit, and name the landform in the words the question uses.
exam_context.frequency: Very common: contour reading appears in almost every map skills question

bronze.display: Worsaw Hill is the rounded hill in the north-east of this map. One of the brown contour lines that circles it carries a printed number. Read that number: it is the height of that line above sea level.
bronze.hint: Look for a small brown number sitting in a gap in one of the lines that ring the hill.

guided_steps.say: Contour numbers are printed on the line itself, sitting in a small gap so the line stays readable.

guided_steps.pre: Look along the top edge for the vertical grid lines. Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Worsaw Hill.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings on this map read 76, 77, 78 from left to right.
guided_steps.done: The hill is now pinned to one column of the grid, so you know exactly where to look.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number on the horizontal grid line immediately below Worsaw Hill.
guided_steps.hint: The northings are printed up the left and right edges.

guided_steps.pre: Now read the brown number printed on the contour line that circles the hill. Type it.
guided_steps.hint: It is printed in brown, in a gap in the line, close to the hill's name.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if that number is a height above sea level in metres, or 2 if it is a distance across the map.
guided_steps.hint: Contour lines join places that are all the same height.
guided_steps.done: Contour numbers are always heights, which is why the same number can turn up in several places on one map.

misconceptions.message: That is a grid line number, not a contour value. Grid numbers sit in blue on the edges of the map, contour values sit in brown on the brown lines.
You read a northing off the side of the map. Contour values are printed along the contour lines themselves.

bronze.display: The contour interval on this map is 10 m, so each brown line is 10 m higher or lower than the one beside it. Worsaw Hill in the north-east is circled by a contour that carries a printed height. What height is the next ring in from that labelled line?
bronze.hint: Moving inwards on a hill means moving uphill, so add the interval once.

guided_steps.say: Rings inside rings mean a hill. The smaller the ring, the higher the ground it encloses.

guided_steps.pre: Find Worsaw Hill in the north-east. Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to its left.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings read 76, 77, 78 from left to right.
guided_steps.done: Hill located, so the lines you read next belong to it and not to its neighbour.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height printed on the labelled contour that circles the hill, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the small brown number sitting in a gap in one of the rings.
guided_steps.done: That printed number is the only height on this hill the map states outright. Everything else is counted from it.

guided_steps.pre: Type the contour interval on this map, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: The interval is given to you in the question.

guided_steps.pre: Moving inwards on a hill is moving uphill. Add one interval to the labelled height. Type the height of the next ring in, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: One step up from the line you have just read.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if the ground inside that ring must be higher than the ring itself, or 2 if it must be lower.
guided_steps.hint: The ring is the last line the land climbs past.
guided_steps.done: The summit is always higher than the highest ring drawn round it, which is why maps often print a spot height as well.

misconceptions.message: You took the interval away instead of adding it. Moving inwards on a hill is moving uphill.
You added the gap between thick index contours instead of the gap between neighbouring lines.

bronze.display: Cow Close Fell, west of the middle of this map, is drawn as a set of closed brown loops, each one inside the last. Which landform does that pattern show?
options: A hill, with its summit inside the smallest loop
A river valley cut into the moor
A flat plain with no slope at all
A vertical cliff face
bronze.hint: Ask yourself whether the ground inside the loops is higher or lower than the ground outside them.

guided_steps.say: Closed loops always mean a change in height, either up to a top or down into a hollow.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Cow Close Fell.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings on this map run 88 to 91 from left to right.
guided_steps.done: Locating the fell first means every reading afterwards comes from the right part of the sheet.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number printed on the thick brown loop that runs round the fell.
guided_steps.hint: It is printed in brown where the thick loop runs along the southern side of the fell.

guided_steps.pre: Type how many smaller loops are drawn inside that thick one.
guided_steps.hint: Look for thinner loops nested inside the thick one and count them.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if the loops get smaller as the land gets higher, or 2 if they get smaller as it gets lower.
guided_steps.hint: The moor falls away from the fell on every side.
guided_steps.done: Smaller loops sitting on higher ground is the test that separates a hill from a hollow.

guided_steps.say: The smallest loop sits on the highest ground, so this is a hill and the top of it lies inside that smallest loop.

misconceptions.message: A valley bends the contours into Vs along a stream. Loops closing on themselves are a different pattern.
A cliff is drawn with its own symbol, not with nested loops. Look at what the loops enclose.

bronze.display: Which grid square contains the smallest contour ring on Cow Close Fell, the ring that marks the top of the fell?
bronze.hint: Read the easting along the bottom edge first, then the northing up the side.

guided_steps.say: A grid square takes its name from the line to its left and the line below it, easting first.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the LEFT of the smallest ring.
guided_steps.hint: Eastings are printed along the top and bottom edges.
guided_steps.done: Left first, then below. That order is the whole rule.

guided_steps.pre: Type the northing of the horizontal grid line immediately BELOW the smallest ring.
guided_steps.hint: Northings read 72, 73, 74 going up the sides of the map.

guided_steps.pre: Put them together, easting first. Type the four figure reference as one number.
guided_steps.hint: Write the two easting digits, then the two northing digits, with nothing between them.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if swapping the two pairs round would land you in a different square, or 2 if it would land you in the same one.
guided_steps.hint: Try reading the digits the other way round and see where they take you.
guided_steps.done: Easting always comes before northing. Swapping them sends you somewhere else entirely.

misconceptions.message: You took the northing from the line above the ring instead of the line below it. A square is named from its bottom left corner.
You took the easting from the line to the right of the ring. A square is named from its bottom left corner.

bronze.display: Grid square 9073, on the floor of Littondale beside the River Skirfare, has no contour lines crossing it at all. What does that tell you about the land there?
options: It is almost flat
It is extremely steep
It is higher than the fells around it
It is completely under water
bronze.hint: A contour is only drawn where the land climbs or drops past that height.

guided_steps.say: Every contour you cross records the land going up or down by one interval.

guided_steps.pre: Find the square with easting 90 down its left side and northing 73 along its base. Type how many brown contour lines cross that square.
guided_steps.hint: Trace each edge of that square in turn and count every brown line that crosses into it.
guided_steps.done: Zero is a real reading here, not a missing one.

guided_steps.pre: Type how many metres the land rises or falls if you cross no contour lines at all.
guided_steps.hint: No lines crossed means no interval gained and none lost.

guided_steps.pre: Now look at square 8973, one square to the west. Type 1 if it has many more contour lines than 9073, or 2 if it has fewer.
guided_steps.hint: The valley side west of Litton is covered in brown lines.
guided_steps.done: Same map, same interval, completely different spacing. That contrast is the relief of the dale.

guided_steps.say: Square 9073 is valley floor, so the land there is almost flat, while the square to its west climbs steeply out of the dale.

misconceptions.message: Missing contour lines do not mean a slope too steep to draw. Think about what a line crossing actually records.
Water is drawn in blue, not left as white space. The river itself is the blue line running through the square.

bronze.display: On this mountain map the thicker brown lines are index contours, and two of them are labelled 650 and 700 to the right of the middle. Look at the slope between those two labels. How many thinner contour lines lie between them?
bronze.hint: Count only the thin lines that sit between the two labelled thick ones, and do not count the thick ones themselves.

guided_steps.say: Index contours are drawn thicker so you can find a height quickly on a crowded slope.

guided_steps.pre: Find the labels 650 and 700 to the right of the middle of the map. Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to their left.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings on this map read 67 to 71 from left to right.
guided_steps.done: Both labels are now pinned to one column of the grid, so you will count on the right slope.

guided_steps.pre: Type the difference between those two heights, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Take the smaller value away from the larger one.
guided_steps.done: Both ends of the count are now fixed, which is what makes the count mean something.

guided_steps.pre: Now follow a straight line from the thick 650 contour across to the thick 700 contour. Type how many thin brown lines you cross on the way.
guided_steps.hint: Cross the slope at right angles to the lines and count each thin line once.

guided_steps.pre: Type how many steps that makes from the 650 line up to the 700 line, counting the step onto the thick line as well.
guided_steps.hint: Four lines in between create one more gap than there are lines.

guided_steps.pre: Share the height difference between those steps. Type the height gap between neighbouring lines, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the height difference by the number of steps.
guided_steps.done: Fifty metres shared over five equal steps gives the contour interval, which is the fact the rest of this lesson rests on.

misconceptions.message: You counted the two labelled thick lines as well. The question asks only for the thin ones between them.
You counted the gaps rather than the lines. Lines and gaps are never the same number.

bronze.display: In grid square 3508, on the slope running east from Heron Pike, the brown contour lines are packed so tightly that they almost touch. What does that spacing tell you about the slope there?
options: The slope is very steep
The slope is very gentle
The land is flat
The land is below sea level
bronze.hint: Close lines mean a lot of height is gained over very little ground.

guided_steps.say: Spacing is the quickest reading on any relief map, and it needs no arithmetic at all.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line on the left-hand side of square 3508.
guided_steps.hint: Eastings run 34, 35, 36 across this map.
guided_steps.done: You are looking at the right square before you judge anything about the slope.

guided_steps.pre: Each contour here is 10 m apart in height. Type how many metres you climb crossing 5 of them.
guided_steps.hint: Five steps of ten metres each.

guided_steps.pre: In this square those 5 lines are crossed in well under half a kilometre. Type 1 if that is a lot of height in a short distance, or 2 if it is a little height over a long distance.
guided_steps.hint: Put the climb you have just worked out next to the ground you cover to gain it, and compare the two.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if lines drawn further apart would mean a gentler slope, or 2 if they would mean a steeper one.
guided_steps.hint: Same height gap, more ground covered between the lines.
guided_steps.done: The height gap never changes, so only the ground covered can change, and that is what spacing shows.

guided_steps.say: Contours packed almost touching in square 3508 mean the slope there is very steep.

misconceptions.message: You have the spacing rule the wrong way round. Think about how far you walk between one line and the next.
Flat land shows as an absence of contour lines, not as a mass of them.

bronze.display: The thick contour ring round Cow Close Fell is labelled 600 m and the contour interval is 10 m. A walker steps off that ring and walks downhill to the very next contour line. What height is that line?
bronze.hint: Downhill means the next line outwards from the ring, one interval lower.

guided_steps.say: Outwards from a summit is downhill. Inwards is uphill. That is the whole direction rule.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Cow Close Fell.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings run 88 to 91 across this map.
guided_steps.done: Fell located, so the ring you read next is certainly the right one.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number printed on the thick ring round the fell, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is printed on the thick loop along the southern side of the fell.
guided_steps.done: Start every height count from a line the map has labelled for you.

guided_steps.pre: Type the contour interval on this map, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: The interval is given in the question.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if walking outwards from the ring goes downhill, or 2 if it goes uphill.
guided_steps.hint: The fell falls away in every direction from its top.

guided_steps.pre: Take one interval off the ring's height. Type the height of the next line out, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: One step down from the labelled ring.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height of the line one more step downhill, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Take another ten metres off.
guided_steps.done: Each step out from a summit takes one interval off, which is how you read any height the map does not print.

misconceptions.message: You added an interval instead of taking one off. Outwards from a summit is downhill.
You stepped by the gap between thick index lines rather than by the gap between neighbouring lines.

silver.display: Two thick index contours on this mountain are labelled 650 and 700, and 4 thinner lines lie between them. Work out the contour interval on this map.
silver.hint: Count the steps from one labelled line to the other, then share the height difference between those steps.

guided_steps.say: The interval is never printed on a map. You work it out from two labelled lines.

guided_steps.pre: Find the two labels to the right of the middle of the map. Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to their left.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings on this map read 67 to 71 from left to right.
guided_steps.done: Labels located, so the lines you count between are the ones the question means.

guided_steps.pre: Type the higher of the two contour values, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: The two labels read 650 and 700.
guided_steps.done: Two known heights on the same slope is all the evidence you need.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height difference between the two labelled lines, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Take the smaller value away from the larger one.

guided_steps.pre: There are 4 thin lines between them. Type how many equal steps that makes from the lower label up to the higher one.
guided_steps.hint: Four lines in between create one more gap than there are lines.

guided_steps.pre: Share the height difference between those steps. Type the contour interval, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the height difference by the number of steps.

guided_steps.pre: Check it. Type the height of the thin line immediately above the 650 line, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Add one interval to 650.
guided_steps.done: One step up from a labelled line landing on a sensible round value is the sign the interval is right.

misconceptions.message: You divided by the number of thin lines instead of the number of steps. Four lines make five gaps.
That is the gap between the two thick lines, not the gap between neighbouring lines.

silver.display: The thick ring on Cow Close Fell is labelled 600 m and the contour interval is 10 m. Two smaller rings are drawn inside it. What height is the smallest ring?
silver.hint: Each ring inwards is one interval higher, so count the rings as steps.

guided_steps.say: Counting inwards from a labelled ring is how you read the top of any hill.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of the fell.
guided_steps.hint: Eastings run 88 to 91 across this map.
guided_steps.done: Fell located, so the rings you count next are certainly the right ones.

guided_steps.pre: Type how many rings are drawn inside the labelled one.
guided_steps.hint: Look for thinner loops nested inside the thick one.

guided_steps.pre: Type how many metres you gain crossing those 2 rings, at 10 m each.
guided_steps.hint: Two steps of ten metres.

guided_steps.pre: Add that gain to the labelled height. Type the height of the smallest ring, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Start at the labelled ring and go up by the amount you have just worked out.

guided_steps.pre: The summit is higher than the smallest ring but lower than the next contour, which is not drawn. Type the height of that undrawn contour, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: One more interval above the smallest ring.
guided_steps.done: The top of the fell is trapped between those two values, which is as precise as contours alone can be.

misconceptions.message: You went up by a single step. Count every ring drawn inside the labelled one.
You went down instead of up. Inwards on a hill is uphill.

silver.display: Greenhead Gill runs across the middle of this map, with its stream drawn in blue. Look carefully at what the brown contours do where they meet that stream. Which landform do they show?
options: A valley, with the contour Vs pointing upstream
A spur, with the contours bulging downhill
A flat plateau
An escarpment with one steep side and one gentle side
silver.hint: Follow one contour line into the stream and watch which way its sharp point faces.

guided_steps.say: Valleys and spurs both bend contours into points. Only the direction of the point tells them apart.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of the Greenhead Gill label.
guided_steps.hint: Eastings run 34, 35, 36 across this map.
guided_steps.done: You are now reading the right stretch of the map rather than a similar looking one nearby.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if the gill itself is drawn in blue, or 2 if it is drawn in brown.
guided_steps.hint: Water is always blue on these maps, relief is always brown.

guided_steps.pre: Follow a contour into the stream. Type 1 if its point faces up the slope towards the higher ground in the north-east, or 2 if it faces down towards Grasmere in the south-west.
guided_steps.hint: Look at the sharp corner each contour makes as it crosses the water.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if a stream runs along the lowest ground it can find, or 2 if it runs along the highest.
guided_steps.hint: Water can only ever run downhill.
guided_steps.done: Because the water takes the lowest line, a contour must bend up the valley to stay at the same height. That bend is the signature you are reading.

guided_steps.say: Sharp points aimed upstream mean the stream has cut down into the land, so this is a valley.

misconceptions.message: A spur bends the contours the other way, out and down the hill. Check which way the points face where the stream crosses.
Flat ground would leave this part of the map almost blank. These lines are close and busy.

silver.display: Stone Arthur is named in the north of this map. Look at the shape the contours make just below the name: they swing out into rounded points that face down the hill, towards the lower ground in the south-west. Which landform is that?
options: A spur
A river valley
A hollow scooped out of the hillside
A flat plateau
silver.hint: Decide whether the high ground is pushing out towards the low ground, or the low ground is biting in.

guided_steps.say: The same points test works for both landforms, so read the direction before you name anything.

guided_steps.pre: Type the northing of the horizontal grid line immediately below the Stone Arthur label.
guided_steps.hint: The northings on this map read 08 and 09.
guided_steps.done: Feature located, so the bends you read next belong to Stone Arthur and not to the ridge behind it.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if the land gets lower towards the south-west corner, where Grasmere village is drawn, or 2 if it gets higher.
guided_steps.hint: Villages sit on low ground, and the contour values fall towards it.

guided_steps.pre: Now look at the points the contours make below Stone Arthur. Type 1 if they face south-west, down towards the village, or 2 if they face north-east.
guided_steps.hint: Follow one contour along until it turns its sharpest corner.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if points facing downhill mean high ground reaching out from the ridge, or 2 if they mean low ground cutting in.
guided_steps.hint: Ask which sort of ground the point is made of, the ground inside the bend or outside it.
guided_steps.done: The bend is made of high ground pushing out, and the low ground lies either side of it.

guided_steps.say: High ground reaching out from a ridge, with lower ground on both sides, is a spur.

misconceptions.message: Valleys bend the contours the opposite way, with the points facing uphill. Check the direction of the bends again.
A hollow of that kind shows as a steep horseshoe of contours round a flat floor, often with a small lake in it. That is not the pattern here.

silver.display: Worsaw Hill in the north-east of this map has contours packed tightly on one side and spread widely on the other. Which statement matches the map?
options: The southern side is steeper, because its contours are closest together
The northern side is steeper, because its contours are closest together
Both sides are equally steep
Neither side of the hill has any slope
silver.hint: Compare how much ground you cross between the same two contour lines on each side of the hill.

guided_steps.say: To compare two slopes fairly, use the same pair of contour lines on both of them.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Worsaw Hill.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings read 76, 77, 78.
guided_steps.done: Hill located, so the two slopes you compare next are the two sides of the same hill.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height printed on the labelled contour that circles the hill, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the brown number printed beside the hill's name.

guided_steps.pre: Walk south from that labelled line, down towards Worsaw End House. Type 1 if the lines below it are close together, or 2 if they are far apart.
guided_steps.hint: Put a fingertip on the labelled line and slide it south, then note how far you go before you meet the next brown line.

guided_steps.pre: Now walk north from the same labelled line, towards the top edge of the map. Type 1 if those lines are close together, or 2 if they are far apart.
guided_steps.hint: Slide from the same labelled line northwards instead, and compare that distance with the one you have just measured.
guided_steps.done: One interval crossed in a few millimetres on one side and across most of a square on the other. That is the comparison the question wants.

guided_steps.say: The same height gap covers far less ground on the southern side, so that is the steeper slope.

misconceptions.message: You matched wide spacing with a steep slope. Think about how far you walk between one line and the next.
Hills are rarely the same on both sides. Compare the spacing directly rather than assuming.

silver.display: A walker starts on the contour labelled 400 m, in the north-west quarter of the map, and climbs to the smallest ring on Cow Close Fell at 620 m. How much height do they gain?
silver.hint: Take the starting height away from the finishing height.

guided_steps.say: Height gain is a subtraction, but only once both heights have been read correctly off the map.

guided_steps.pre: Find the label 400 in the north-west quarter of the map. Type the northing of the horizontal grid line immediately below it.
guided_steps.hint: Northings read 72, 73, 74 going up the sides of the map.
guided_steps.done: Start point located, so you are subtracting from a height you can actually point at.

guided_steps.pre: Type the starting height, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the value printed on the contour where the walker sets off.

guided_steps.pre: Type the finishing height, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: The height of the smallest ring is given in the question.

guided_steps.pre: Take the start away from the finish. Type the height gained, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the smaller height from the larger one.

guided_steps.pre: At 10 m per contour, type how many contour lines the walker crosses on the way up.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the height gained by the contour interval.
guided_steps.done: The line count and the subtraction have to agree, because they are the same climb counted two ways.

misconceptions.message: You added the two heights together instead of finding the difference between them.
That is the number of contour lines crossed, not the height gained. Each line is worth one interval.

silver.display: On the southern slope of Worsaw Hill, below the contour labelled 200 m, four thin lines are drawn and then another thick index contour. Index contours on this map come every 50 m. What height is that lower thick line?
silver.hint: Index lines come every fifty metres, and heading downhill means going down by that amount.

guided_steps.say: Thick index lines are a ladder. Once you know one rung, the rest come fifty metres at a time.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number on the horizontal grid line immediately below Worsaw Hill.
guided_steps.hint: The northings on this map read 42 and 43.
guided_steps.done: Hill located, so the thick line you read next is the one on its southern slope.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height printed on the thick contour that circles the hill, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the brown number printed beside the hill's name.

guided_steps.pre: Type the gap between index contours on this map, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: The index spacing is given in the question.

guided_steps.pre: Heading south from the hill is heading downhill. Take one index gap off. Type the height of the lower thick line, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the index gap from the labelled height.

guided_steps.pre: Check it against the thin lines: at 10 m each, type how many thin lines should lie between those two thick ones.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the index gap by the interval, then take one off for the step onto the thick line.
guided_steps.done: Four thin lines fit a fifty metre gap at ten metres a line, and four is exactly what the map draws there.

misconceptions.message: You added the index gap instead of taking it off. The land falls away to the south here.
You stepped by the gap between neighbouring lines rather than the gap between thick index lines.

gold.display: On the western flank of Cow Close Fell, the contour labelled 550 m and the thick 600 m ring lie about 0.5 km apart on the ground. Calculate the average gradient of that slope in metres per km.
gold.hint: Divide the height climbed by the distance travelled, keeping the distance in km.

guided_steps.say: Gradient is height gained divided by ground covered. The units you divide in are the units you answer in.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Cow Close Fell.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings run 88 to 91 across this map.
guided_steps.done: Fell located, so the slope you measure is the western flank and not another one.

guided_steps.pre: Type the lower of the two contour heights named, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the labelled line out to the west of the fell.
guided_steps.done: Both ends of the slope are now fixed to labelled lines, so the climb is a fact rather than an estimate.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height climbed between the two lines, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Take the lower height away from the higher one.

guided_steps.pre: Type the horizontal distance between them, in km.
guided_steps.hint: The distance is given in the question.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the height climbed by the distance. Type the gradient in metres per km.
guided_steps.hint: Fifty metres of climb shared over half a kilometre of ground.

guided_steps.pre: Check it. At that gradient, type how many metres you would climb over a full 2 km.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the gradient by two.
guided_steps.done: Doubling the distance doubles the climb, which is exactly what an average gradient promises.

misconceptions.message: You divided the distance by the height. Gradient puts the height on top.
You used the distance as if it were a whole kilometre. Half the ground for the same climb makes a steeper figure.

gold.display: The same slope on the western flank of Cow Close Fell climbs 50 m over 0.5 km. Gradients are often written as a ratio, 1 in something. Work out that figure: this slope is 1 in what?
gold.hint: Turn the distance into metres first, then work out how far you travel along for each metre you go up.

guided_steps.say: A ratio gradient compares metres up with metres along, so both have to be in metres.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Cow Close Fell.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings run 88 to 91 across this map.
guided_steps.done: Same slope as before, located the same way, so the two answers can be compared.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height climbed, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the gap between the two contour values named in the question.
guided_steps.done: The rise is already in metres, so only the distance needs converting.

guided_steps.pre: Type the horizontal distance, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: There are one thousand metres in a kilometre, so half a kilometre is half of that.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the distance along by the height up. Type the answer.
guided_steps.hint: Five hundred shared into fifty.

guided_steps.pre: Check it. Type how many metres along you would travel while climbing just 1 m at that gradient.
guided_steps.hint: The ratio is the metres along for every single metre up.
guided_steps.done: One metre up for that many along is the same slope written a different way, so the two readings agree.

misconceptions.message: You divided the height by the distance. A ratio counts the metres along for each single metre up.
You kept the distance in kilometres. Both parts of a ratio must be in the same unit.

gold.display: Imagine drawing a cross section along a straight west to east line that starts on the 550 m contour, passes over the top of Cow Close Fell and carries on down the far side. Which description matches the profile you would draw?
options: It climbs to a rounded top, then falls away on the far side
It drops into a V, then climbs back out
It stays at the same height the whole way
It climbs in one step and then stays level
gold.hint: Read the contour values along the line in order and note where they stop rising and start falling.

guided_steps.say: A cross section is only the contour values met along a line, plotted in the order you meet them.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Cow Close Fell.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings run 88 to 91 across this map.
guided_steps.done: The line of section now has a fixed place on the map, which is what makes the profile repeatable.

guided_steps.pre: Type the value of the labelled contour the line starts on, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is printed on the thick line to the west of the fell.
guided_steps.done: The line now has a fixed starting height, so every later value can be compared with it.

guided_steps.pre: Type the value of the thick ring the line crosses next, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: It is the labelled ring drawn round the fell.

guided_steps.pre: Type the value of the smallest ring the line crosses at the top, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Count the rings inside the thick one, one interval each.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if the same contour values appear again on the eastern side of the top, or 2 if brand new higher values appear.
guided_steps.hint: Look at the rings east of the summit and read their values.
guided_steps.done: Values repeating on the far side is what makes a profile symmetrical enough to call a top rather than a step.

guided_steps.say: The values rise to a maximum at the smallest ring and then repeat downwards, which draws a rounded top with a fall away on the far side.

misconceptions.message: A V shape needs the values to fall first and rise afterwards. Check the order in which you meet them.
The line does not stop at the top. Follow it down the eastern side and see what the values do.

gold.display: On the eastern side of this map the index contours are labelled 450, 500, 550 and 600. The contour interval is 10 m. A walker climbs from the 450 m line up to the 600 m line. How many contour lines do they cross, counting the 600 line but not the 450 line they start on?
gold.hint: Work out the height climbed first, then see how many ten metre steps fit into it.

guided_steps.say: On a crowded slope, arithmetic is safer than counting lines one by one with your eye.

guided_steps.pre: Type the easting of the vertical grid line immediately to the left of those labels.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings run 34, 35, 36 across this map.
guided_steps.done: Labels located, so both ends of the climb sit on the slope the question means.

guided_steps.pre: Type the highest of the labelled index values on the eastern side of the map, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Four index contours are labelled down that side: 450, 500, 550 and 600.
guided_steps.done: Both ends of the climb are labelled lines, so the height gained is certain.

guided_steps.pre: Type the height climbed between the two labelled lines, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Take the lower value away from the higher one.

guided_steps.pre: Type the contour interval, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: The interval is given in the question.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the climb by the interval. Type how many lines are crossed.
guided_steps.hint: Each line crossed is worth one interval of climb.

guided_steps.pre: Check it with the thick lines: type how many index contours the walker crosses, counting the 600 line but not the 450 one.
guided_steps.hint: Index lines come every 50 m.
guided_steps.done: Three thick lines inside fifteen lines in total is one thick line every five, which is exactly how the map is drawn.

misconceptions.message: You counted the line you set off from. The count starts above it.
You divided by the gap between thick lines instead of by the gap between neighbouring lines.

gold.display: Worsaw Hill in the north-east of this map is circled by a contour labelled 200 m, and the interval is 10 m. Closed rings are drawn inside that labelled contour. The summit is higher than the highest ring drawn, but the next contour above it is not drawn anywhere on the hill. What is the value of that undrawn contour?
gold.hint: Count every closed ring inside the labelled contour, then go one interval past the smallest.

guided_steps.say: The highest ring drawn sets a floor for the summit. The first undrawn contour sets the ceiling.

guided_steps.pre: Type the number on the vertical grid line immediately to the left of Worsaw Hill.
guided_steps.hint: The eastings read 76, 77, 78.
guided_steps.done: Hill located, so you are reasoning about the right summit and not one of its neighbours.

guided_steps.pre: Type how many closed rings are drawn inside the labelled 200 m contour.
guided_steps.hint: One is a large loop round the whole top. Look again very close to the summit before you settle on a count.
guided_steps.done: Small summit rings are easy to miss, and missing one costs you a whole interval.

guided_steps.pre: Each ring inwards is one interval up. Type the height of the highest ring drawn, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: Start at the labelled height and add the interval once for each ring you counted.

guided_steps.pre: Add one more interval. Type the value of the first contour that is not drawn, in metres.
guided_steps.hint: One step above the highest ring.

guided_steps.pre: Type 1 if the summit must be lower than that undrawn contour, or 2 if it could be higher than it.
guided_steps.hint: Ask what the map would have done if the land reached that height.
guided_steps.done: If the ground reached that height the map would have drawn the ring, so the summit is trapped between the two values.

misconceptions.message: You have missed one of the closed rings inside the labelled contour. Look again at the ground closest to the summit and recount.
You went down a step instead of up. The undrawn line lies above the highest ring, not below it.
You added the gap between thick index lines rather than a single interval.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Read what the map already prints: contour numbers, the rings round a hill, and whether the lines are packed or spread.
problem_bank.silver_description: Work out heights the map does not print, using the contour interval and the thicker index contours.
problem_bank.gold_description: Turn contour patterns into gradients and cross sections, in metres per km or as a 1 in ratio.

worked_examples.question: Read the height of the contour line that circles Worsaw Hill on this map.

steps.label: Step 1: Locate the hill
steps.content: Worsaw Hill is named in the north-east of the extract, to the right of the easting line 77 and above the northing line 43.

steps.label: Step 2: Find the printed number
steps.content: Contour values are printed in brown, in a small gap in the line itself. Beside the hill's name a thicker brown line carries the number 200.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The line is at 200 m above sea level. Every point along it is the same height.

worked_examples.question: Work out the contour interval used on this mountain map.

steps.label: Step 1: Find two labelled lines
steps.content: To the right of the middle of the extract, two thicker index contours are labelled 650 and 700.

steps.label: Step 2: Count the thin lines between them
steps.content: Crossing straight from one to the other you pass 4 thinner lines. That makes 5 equal steps from 650 up to 700.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 700 − 650 = 50 m, shared over 5 steps: 10 m interval.

worked_examples.question: The 550 m contour and the 600 m ring on the western flank of Cow Close Fell are about 0.5 km apart. Give the gradient in metres per km and as a ratio.

steps.label: Step 1: Read both heights
steps.content: The labelled contour west of the fell reads 550 and the thick ring round the fell reads 600, so the climb is 50 m.

steps.label: Step 2: Divide by the distance
steps.content: Gradient is the climb divided by the distance, with the distance left in km: 50 ÷ 0.5.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 100 m per km. As a ratio: 0.5 km is 500 m, and 500 ÷ 50 = 1 in 10.
